Hospital Appointment Management and Patient Attendance Analysis Using R

Attendance patterns and probability prediction using Random Forest and XGBoost

Harshit Srinivasa Prasad

15 October 2026

1 Abstract

Missed hospital appointments create uncertainty in scheduling and can leave capacity unused. This study analyses historical appointment records and estimates attendance probabilities using Random Forest and XGBoost. The working file contains 53,978 appointments before cleaning and 53,976 afterward. Preparation includes checking records, correcting target labels, converting dates and calculating waiting days. Patients remain separate across training, validation and testing partitions. Validation F1 selects follow-up thresholds, while test evaluation includes precision, recall, F1 and Brier score. Random Forest obtains test F1 0.4450 and XGBoost obtains 0.4468. The final demonstration reports attending and missing probabilities for a fictional appointment. The results support reminder prioritisation as a research prototype. They do not establish that reminders improve attendance or that the model transfers to other hospitals. Incomplete source coverage and the absence of several personal and operational factors limit the findings.

2 Introduction

2.1 Background

Hospital staff must plan appointments despite uncertainty about patient attendance. Historical records can identify patterns and support estimates of missed-appointment risk.

2.2 Problem statement

How can historical patient and appointment information help identify appointments at higher risk of being missed, while reporting the probability of attendance?

2.3 Objectives

  1. Prepare appointment records for analysis.
  2. Compare attendance across age groups, gender, waiting periods and SMS status.
  3. Train Random Forest and XGBoost probability models.
  4. Select follow-up thresholds using validation data and evaluate test performance.
  5. Demonstrate attending and missing probabilities for a new fictional patient.

2.4 Scope

The implementation analyses attendance and predicts outcomes. It does not book, cancel or reschedule appointments, and it does not send SMS messages. The SMS indicator must already be available at the time a prediction is made.

3 Data

3.1 Source and variables

The working file is KaggleV2-May-2016.csv, associated with the Medical Appointment No Shows dataset. Each row represents an appointment; patients can appear more than once. Counts below describe the imported working file, which may be a subset of the original dataset.

Variable Description
PatientId, AppointmentID Patient and appointment identifiers
Gender, Age Recorded demographic details
ScheduledDay, AppointmentDay Booking and appointment dates
Neighbourhood Recorded neighbourhood
Scholarship Welfare programme indicator
Hipertension, Diabetes, Alcoholism Recorded health indicators
Handcap Recorded disability category
SMS_received Recorded SMS reminder indicator; does not prove reading
verification Target renamed from No-show, recoded as Attended or Missed
WaitingDays Appointment date minus booking date in calendar days

The original No-show = Yes means Missed, while No means Attended.

4 Methodology

4.1 Overall workflow

  1. Import and inspect the CSV.
  2. Clean records and calculate waiting days.
  3. Separate patients into training, validation and testing partitions.
  4. Fit Random Forest and XGBoost on model-training records.
  5. Select thresholds on validation records.
  6. Evaluate fixed models and thresholds on testing records.
  7. Interpret attendance patterns and demonstrate a new appointment prediction.
  8. Save models, results and report data.

4.2 Data cleaning

The notebook checks missing values, duplicate rows and data types. It removes negative ages, converts date fields and excludes invalid waiting periods. Age zero remains valid for infants. Repeated patients remain in the dataset because separate appointments are legitimate observations.

4.4 Training validation and testing

Approximately 80% of patients enter the outer training partition. Of those, approximately 20% enter validation. The remaining patients form the test set. Appointment proportions differ because patients have different record counts.

4.5 Models and evaluation

Model Configuration Evaluation
Random Forest 300 trees, mtry 3, minimum node size 20, probability forest Precision, recall, F1, accuracy, Brier score
XGBoost Binary logistic, eta 0.05, depth 4, child weight 10, row and column sampling 0.8 Same test metrics; validation log loss for early stopping

Both models use seed 33. XGBoost allows up to 500 rounds and stops after 30 rounds without validation improvement. Thresholds from 0.01 to 0.99 maximise validation F1. The test set does not determine thresholds. Random Forest uses the method implemented in ranger (Wright and Ziegler, 2017); XGBoost follows the boosting system described by Chen and Guestrin (2016).

5 Exploratory data analysis

5.1 Outcome distribution

Attendance distribution
Outcome Count Percent
Attended 42599 78.92
Missed 11377 21.08

The missed rate is 21.08%. A model can obtain high accuracy by predicting the majority class, so missed-class recall matters.

5.2 Patient and appointment groups

Percentages compare groups of unequal sizes. These are descriptive associations, not evidence that a characteristic causes missed appointments. SMS groups may differ in waiting periods and other factors.

6 Classification results

6.1 XGBoost learning curve

6.2 Validation thresholds

Validation threshold selection
Model Threshold Accuracy Precision Recall F1
Random Forest 0.22 0.5999 0.3142 0.7599 0.4446
XGBoost 0.24 0.6242 0.3237 0.7191 0.4465

The follow-up thresholds are 0.22 for Random Forest and 0.24 for XGBoost. A follow-up flag can occur below 50% missing probability. It does not imply that missing is the more likely outcome.

6.3 Test metrics and baseline

Test performance
Model Threshold Accuracy Precision Recall F1 BrierScore
Random Forest 0.22 0.6029 0.3160 0.7522 0.4450 0.1516
XGBoost 0.24 0.6260 0.3252 0.7137 0.4468 0.1505
Simple baselines
Metric Value
Always-attend accuracy 0.7884
Constant-risk Brier score 0.1668

Precision is the proportion of flagged appointments actually missed. Recall is the proportion of missed appointments identified. F1 balances both, while Brier score measures squared probability error. Lower Brier score is better.

8 New patient prediction

The details below represent a fictional patient, with no known actual outcome.

New appointment details
Age Gender Scholarship Hipertension Diabetes Alcoholism Handcap SMS_received WaitingDays
28 M 0 0 1 0 4 0 20
Attendance probabilities and follow-up
Model Attending_Percent Missing_Percent More_Probable_Outcome Follow_Up_Flag
Random Forest 72.36 27.64 Attended Prioritize reminder or confirmation
XGBoost 60.60 39.40 Attended Prioritize reminder or confirmation

Attending and missing probabilities total approximately 100% after rounding. The more probable outcome uses 50%, while the reminder flag uses the selected validation threshold. Staff could use flags to prioritise confirmation calls. This demonstration does not validate the model or establish an operational benefit.

9 Model comparison and discussion

  • Random Forest: precision 31.60%, recall 75.22%, F1 0.4450, Brier score 0.1516.

  • XGBoost: precision 32.52%, recall 71.37%, F1 0.4468, Brier score 0.1505.

The analysis addresses attendance patterns and implements both probability models. Lower thresholds prioritise recall but create more unnecessary calls. The confusion matrices quantify this workload. Small differences in F1 do not establish a statistically reliable winner. The new-patient output demonstrates the interface between patient details, probability estimates and follow-up flags.

10 Limitations

  • The working CSV may be a subset; its coverage must be documented.
  • Patient-separated testing does not establish performance on future dates or other hospitals.
  • Transport barriers, urgency and other relevant factors are absent.
  • SMS status does not establish reading and must be known at prediction time.
  • Threshold selection maximises F1 rather than hospital benefit or call capacity.
  • Probability calibration and subgroup performance need further assessment.
  • The test set was inspected during development; external evaluation would provide stronger evidence.
  • Feature importance and descriptive graphs show associations, not causation.

11 Conclusion

The project prepares appointment records, analyses attendance patterns and fits Random Forest and XGBoost. Validation selects follow-up thresholds, and test results quantify probability quality and missed-appointment detection. The final output provides attending and missing probabilities with a separate reminder flag. This is a research prototype; practical use needs external validation and an assessment of follow-up costs and benefits.

11.1 Future work

  • Verify complete source coverage and evaluate later appointments.
  • Assess calibration and performance across patient groups.
  • Choose thresholds according to reminder capacity and costs.
  • Add an input interface and test whether targeted reminders improve attendance.

12 Reproducibility

This report renders saved experiment results without retraining models. Keep report_data.rds beside the report. To reproduce training, use the Colab notebook with the same CSV, split seed and package versions. Saving results does not by itself create Git history; version control must be maintained separately.

Render with params = list(show_code = TRUE) to display analysis code.
